title: Inflation
examples: What is the difference between demand-pull and cost-push inflation?
How does the Consumer Price Index help us measure inflation?
Can high inflation be good for an economy?

explain.say: Today we are learning about inflation in economics. Inflation means that prices for goods and services are rising. This means that your money buys less than it used to.

draw.text: Inflation: Rising prices, less buying power.

explain.say: We measure inflation using something called the Consumer Price Index. This index tracks the average price change of many goods. It helps us see how much the cost of living is changing.
One major cause of inflation is an increase in supply costs. When the cost of making things goes up, businesses often raise their selling prices. This is called cost-push inflation.

draw.text: Cost-Push: Input costs rise, prices rise.

explain.say: Another cost is energy prices. If the cost of oil or electricity suddenly increases, it raises the cost for almost every business. This cost increase gets passed on to you, the consumer.

draw.text: Energy costs affect all goods and services.

explain.say: The cost of inflation is reduced purchasing power. If your wages do not rise as fast as prices, you can buy fewer things. This affects household budgets greatly.

draw.text: Inflation reduces what money can buy.

explain.say: In everyday life, think about petrol prices. If the cost of oil rises sharply, it increases the cost for buses and cars. This higher cost is often reflected in the ticket price you pay.

draw.text: Petrol price rise affects all travel costs.

faq.q: What is the difference between inflation and deflation?
faq.a: Inflation means prices are generally rising over time. Deflation means that prices are generally falling over time. Both changes affect how much your money is worth.
asks: What is the opposite of inflation?

faq.q: Does inflation always mean the economy is doing badly?
faq.a: Not necessarily. A little bit of inflation is normal for a healthy economy. However, very high inflation can signal serious problems.
asks: What is the ideal inflation rate?

faq.q: How does the CPI calculate the average price change?
faq.a: The CPI takes a 'basket' of goods that typical households buy. It then calculates the weighted average change in the cost of that basket.
asks: What is a standard basket of goods?

faq.q: Why is a rise in energy costs considered cost-push?
faq.a: Because the cost increase comes from the supply side, specifically energy inputs. Businesses must pay more for energy, which pushes up their costs.
asks: What is the source of cost-push inflation?

faq.q: If my wages rise by three percent, but inflation is five percent, what happens?
faq.a: You are effectively losing two percent of your buying power. This means your real income has decreased, which is a negative outcome.
asks: How do I calculate my loss in buying power?

facts: Inflation is a sustained increase in the general price level.
The Consumer Price Index tracks the cost of a standard basket of goods.
Cost-push inflation happens when the cost of inputs rises.
High inflation erodes the real value of money.

quiz.say: If the price of bread goes from two pounds to three pounds, what is this showing?
quiz.why: The price increase shows that money buys less bread than before, which is the definition of inflation.

wrong.0: A supply shock is a sudden event, but this is just a general price change.
wrong.1: Equilibrium means prices are stable, but the price clearly rose.
wrong.3: Deflation means prices are falling, but here the price went up.

quiz.say: If the cost of steel rises, leading to higher car prices, what type of inflation is this?
quiz.why: Because the cost of a key input, steel, has increased, pushing up the final price.

wrong.1: Demand-pull relates to too much money chasing too few goods, not input costs.
wrong.2: Hyperinflation is an extreme, rapid rate of price increase, not just a cost rise.
wrong.3: Stagflation involves high prices and low growth, but the cause here is specific to input costs.

quiz.say: If your salary increases by four percent, but the CPI shows a three percent rise, what is your real income change?

options.show: A real income increase of one percent
options.say: A real income increase of one percent

options.show: A real income decrease of one percent
options.say: A real income decrease of one percent

quiz.why: Your wages rose faster than the cost of living, so your actual purchasing power increased.

wrong.1: This would happen if inflation was higher than your wage rise.
wrong.2: This would mean your wages perfectly matched the rate of inflation.
wrong.3: This ignores the fact that prices are also rising, which reduces your buying power.
